documents.abstract: The Analog Electronic Technology course is concept-intensive, and its circuit analysis methods are flexible. A relatively common difficulty among students is that “single-point knowledge can still be mastered, but the overall context is difficult to connect.” In teaching, problems such as linear content organization, unified learning support, a long feedback cycle, and mismatch between resources and needs have existed for a long time. In response, this study takes Outcome-Based Education (OBE) as the basic guidance, connects the structured organization ability of the smart knowledge graph with the dialogue interaction ability of the artificial intelligence (AI) agent, and constructs a blended teaching model driven by an AI smart knowledge graph. Starting from graduation requirements and course objectives, knowledge points are reversely decomposed, four types of associations, namely prerequisite, parallel, causal, and application associations, are sorted out, and a three-layer smart knowledge graph organized in five levels of “course-module-chapter-knowledge point-sub-knowledge point” is formed. On this basis, an AI teaching agent is developed to undertake preview guidance, in-class question answering, homework correction, learning situation analysis, and other work. The teaching process is then rearranged according to the three stages of before class, in class, and after class. A one-semester comparative practice shows that the final average score of the experimental class is 8.7 points higher than that of the control class, the score difference in comprehensive questions is especially obvious, the proportion of students independently completing design experiments has increased, and the dispersion of scores has also narrowed. The relevant practices have certain reference value for the intelligent transformation of basic courses in electronic information majors, but the scope of application of the conclusions is still limited by the sample size and implementation rounds.

Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to improve the efficiency of healthcare, but its integration in sub-Saharan Africa faces structural constraints. This exploratory study analyzes the perceptions, expectations, and fears of healthcare professionals in the Ibanda Health Zone (Bukavu, DRC) to document the professional acceptability of these technologies. Methods: The study used a mixed-methods approach: the qualitative exploratory component was based on semi-structured interviews with 11 professionals (physicians, nurses, technicians, managers). The data underwent inductive thematic analysis supplemented by descriptive frequency quantification. Results: Overall attitudes toward AI are favorable, albeit with certain conditions. Despite a predominantly basic or informal understanding of AI (81.8%), perceived benefits include improved diagnostics (72.7%) and data management (63.6%). However, major obstacles persist: lack of formal training (81.8%), internet instability (72.7%), and concerns about the reliability of results (54.5%). AI acceptance is high but conditional, revealing a gap between technological promises and realities on the ground. Training (cited by 90.9% of participants) emerges as the central lever and an ethical prerequisite for safe use. Conclusion : The integration of AI at Ibanda cannot be reduced to a technical issue; it requires strengthening basic infrastructure, a clear regulatory framework, and active involvement of caregivers in the design of tools.

documents.abstract: This study, grounded in the psychology of working theory (PWT) and self-determination theory (SDT), examined how working conditions shape musicians’ experiences of decent work, intrinsic motivation, artistic identity, creative engagement, and psychological well-being. Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted with Portuguese musicians, including both freelancers and those with stable contracts. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four overarching themes: (a) job security and precarity, (b) intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and creative engagement, (c) artistic identity and purpose, and (d) well-being and mental health. The findings show that freelance instability undermines security, constrains creative risk-taking, and increases stress, whereas financial and institutional stability supports intrinsic motivation, reinforces artistic identity, and enables creative exploration. Features associated with intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement, persistence, and psychological investment in creative tasks were observed across both groups. Autonomy itself sustained engagement for some freelancers, highlighting personal resilience and self-directed creativity. The results underscore the interplay between structural conditions (PWT) and individual motivations (SDT), showing that sustainable work environments foster well-being and high-quality creative output. The study provides practical implications for policies, education, and organizational strategies to support healthier, more productive artistic ecosystems.

This qualitative descriptive study explored how nurse educators at Olivarez College Tagaytay, Cavite, accepted and integrated generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in nursing education and developed an evidence-informed action plan. Eight purposively selected nurse educators who had used GenAI in teaching participated in semi-structured, in-depth interviews during August 2026. The interview guide was expert-validated, and recordings were transcribed and examined through Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. Data collection occurred in three waves; 125 codes were organized into six themes and 16 subthemes. The themes were unplanned entry into a necessary technology; conditional acceptance anchored in professional judgment; adapting under generational pressure; integration at the preparation stage; safeguarding learning through vigilance and assessment redesign; and enablement by leadership without written policy. Educators perceived GenAI as useful for preparing lessons, cases, questions, and simplified learning materials but insisted on verifying outputs and protecting clinical judgment, empathy, academic integrity, and patient safety. Integration remained largely preparatory and individualized, while participants described uneven digital confidence, assessment vulnerabilities, personal subscription costs, and the absence of consistent written rules despite administrative encouragement. The findings indicate a gap between conditional acceptance and systematic pedagogical integration. A five-component action plan addressing governance, differentiated faculty development, assessment integrity, student AI literacy, and technical access was proposed, not evaluated. The study contributes institution-specific evidence to responsible GenAI adoption in nursing education.

documents.abstract: Abstract Research on large language model failure predominantly assesses models in single exchanges and isolation: a prompted model, a scored output, and a reported error rate. The focus on single exchanges and isolation belies these current models’ professional use. Clinicians, attorneys, analysts, educators, and researchers work across extended sessions, and each output becomes the context for the next, while the final product carries a human signature. A test that scores a single response most likely will not reveal the behaviors that emerge under those conditions. This paper describes seven candidate failure patterns identified in exploratory, single-author observation of extended sessions on three commercial AI platforms: recognition without correction, compounding rather than isolation of errors, halo effect from real anchors, unreliable self-explanation, degradation across long sessions, exculpatory framing under confrontation, and sycophancy and confirmation bias amplification. Several are consistent with findings already established in the machine learning literature. Overall, the patterns describe a systemic failure profile that lower hallucination rates do not address because the concern lies in how the system handles errors once they exist. The systemic failure profile carries significant ethical consequences and concerns, since failures cascade to final approval; the duty to verify applies to any domain where a person approves LLM output.

documents.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now part of routine academic work in health professions education, often outpacing institutional policy, infrastructure, and training. We describe how educators and trainees use GenAI, their concerns, and the institutional support they perceive, and examine whether prior AI training and frequency of use are associated with these perceptions. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey (August–November 2025) of faculty, clinicians, staff, and trainees involved in health professions education across the United States, recruited through professional networks. Ten items on a 0–5 agreement scale captured attitudes, concerns, trust in AI accuracy, and perceived institutional resources. We used descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, Mann–Whitney U tests with Holm correction, and multivariable ordinal logistic regression with sensitivity analyses. Results: Of 211 responses, 183 respondents with documented consent were analyzed (76.5% faculty; 48 named institutions). Nearly all had used GenAI (98.9%), and 78.1% used it at least weekly, most often for writing or editing (77.6%). Half or more agreed or strongly agreed that they were concerned about academic integrity (58.5%), data privacy (56.3%), and professional accountability (50.8%), yet only 14.2% agreed or strongly agreed that they trust the accuracy of AI-generated content. Only 24.0% agreed or strongly agreed that their institution provides the resources they need (M = 2.51). Among respondents with elevated concern, 73.8% still used GenAI weekly or more. Any AI training (39.9%, mostly informal workshops) was associated with greater comfort and perceived institutional resources, but not significantly with trust or any concern. More frequent use was independently associated with greater trust (OR 4.93, 95% CI 2.46–9.86) and fewer ethical concerns (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.16–0.61), and both associations held in sensitivity analyses. Privacy concern was not associated with use frequency. Conclusions: GenAI has become part of routine work for most health professions educators, yet it coexists with substantial concerns about privacy, integrity, and accountability. Training was associated with comfort but not with lower concern, suggesting that faculty development alone is unlikely to be sufficient; institutions may need to pair it with the governance, data protection, and approved tools that individual training cannot provide.

documents.abstract: Transformasi ekonomi digital meningkatkan volume, kecepatan, dan kompleksitas informasi yang harus diproses organisasi dalam pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Perkembangan artificial intelligence (AI) kemudian menggeser fungsi teknologi dari sekadar pendukung keputusan menuju penguatan kapasitas kognitif, kolaborasi manusia–AI, dan keterlibatan yang lebih luas dalam proses keputusan. Penelitian ini bertujuan mensintesis perkembangan peran AI dalam pengambilan keputusan bisnis dan mengidentifikasi bagaimana perubahan tersebut membentuk arsitektur pengambilan keputusan baru dalam ekonomi digital. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif melalui qualitative thematic literature review. Penelusuran literatur dilakukan melalui basis data Scopus dan menghasilkan 1.326 rekaman awal, kemudian 1.303 rekaman unik. Setelah penyaringan akses full-text dan relevansi substantif, diperoleh 45 artikel untuk pemeriksaan penuh, dengan 38 artikel ditetapkan sebagai corpus inti. Analisis tematik menghasilkan empat tema utama: (1) pergeseran dari AI decision support menuju AI augmentation; (2) kolaborasi manusia–AI dan rekonstruksi pertimbangan manajerial; (3) perluasan peran generative AI dalam proses pengambilan keputusan; dan (4) trust, governance, serta batas kewenangan keputusan AI. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa transformasi AI tidak semata-mata mengarah pada penggantian manusia, tetapi pada reorganisasi pembagian kerja kognitif dan kewenangan keputusan antara manusia dan mesin. Berdasarkan temuan tersebut, penelitian mengusulkan konsep AI-Augmented Business Decision Architecture sebagai kerangka untuk memahami transformasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis di era ekonomi digital.

documents.abstract: AI in education is changing faster than conventional academic publishing can follow. A paper that takes a year to reach print may describe tools, policies and evidence that have already been superseded. This article describes an experiment in doing things differently. Over a single evening in October 2026, a practitioner-scholar and an AI agent turned a body of 81 long-form newsletter articles on AI in education into ten thematic papers, each with original figures, verified references and an open disclosure of how it was made, and published them in Future Science Archives, a non-profit, open-review archive. The article sets out the motivation for the experiment, including the author's long interest in educational innovation and his concerns about the economics of academ‐ ic publishing. It describes the venue and its strengths and limitations, the source corpus, the workflow and the division of labour between human and AI, and the verification process, which found and corrected more than two dozen errors, unverifiable claims and one retracted study carried over from the newsletters. It reports the actual publication timeline. It then discusses the risks of the approach, including "research slop", weakened rigour and researchers becoming editors of machine-written text, and argues that these risks are real but manageable when the human remains responsible for judgement and the process is transparent. It closes with a replicable workflow for others.

Medical education is evolving rapidly alongside the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs). Continuing medical education (CME) has traditionally relied on educational modalities sometimes conceptualized as the “three P’s” of Posters, Podium presentations, and Publications, later expanded into the “seven P’s” with the addition of Podcasts, Play, Peer-to-peer learning, and Patient interactions. This commentary proposes Prompting as an eighth “P” of CME, reflecting the growing importance of effectively interacting with AI systems in clinical and academic practice. Prompting refers to the process of crafting and refining instructions that guide AI-generated outputs. The quality, specificity, and contextual framing of prompts substantially influence the accuracy and usefulness of responses generated by LLMs. Emerging evidence suggests that prompting is a learnable skill that can improve educational and clinical utility without requiring advanced technical expertise. This commentary reviews key prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, role-based, chain-of-thought, and iterative prompting, and discusses their relevance to healthcare providers. Applications across clinical care, medical education, patient communication, administration, and research are explored. Potential benefits include generating differential diagnoses, summarizing medical literature, creating educational materials, supporting clinical simulations, and improving patient-facing communication. The commentary also addresses important risks associated with LLM use, including hallucinations, automation bias, and overreliance on AI-generated content. Ultimately, prompting is framed not only as a mechanism for learning through AI systems, but also as a modern medical literacy competency that healthcare providers must actively develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education.

documents.abstract: Abstract The widespread adoption of video conferencing (VC) platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic has transformed synchronous higher education, yet sustaining student engagement in such environments remains a persistent challenge, particularly in creative disciplines. This study investigated the effectiveness of three gamification elements included animated badges, experience points, and level upgrades in enhancing behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement within a synchronous VC learning context. Guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study employed a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group design involving 124 first-year undergraduate graphic design students from three public universities in China. Participants were assigned to a non-gamified control group or one of three gamified conditions and completed pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring multidimensional engagement. Paired t-test analyses revealed statistically significant improvements across all engagement dimensions in the gamified groups (p < 0.001), while the control group exhibited minimal or no meaningful change. Experience points produced the most consistent gains across behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement, whereas level upgrades yielded the strongest effects on deep cognitive processing and metacognitive regulation. Animated badges were particularly effective in enhancing emotional engagement and learning enjoyment. One-way ANOVA results further indicated clear performance differentiation between gamified and non-gamified conditions. These findings displayed that well-designed gamification mechanisms can substantially enhance engagement in synchronous VC environments by supporting learners’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The study contributes empirical evidence to gamification and online learning literature and offers practical guidance for educators and platform designers seeking to improve motivation, interaction, and learning quality in real-time digital instruction.

Ethical principles are essential to the responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare. This study examines the explicit lexical representation of predefined ethical themes in a selected corpus of 73 healthcare-AI publications. A nine-theme ethical codebook was developed from institutional guidance and relevant peer-reviewed literature. The study applied NLP-supported full-text analysis, inductive topic modeling, deductive codebook-guided content analysis, theme-based corpus analysis, and paper-level statistical comparison. The findings showed substantial variation in thematic representation. Fairness, accountability, and privacy received the strongest overall representation. Fairness had the highest raw keyword frequency, whereas accountability had the highest median adjusted occurrence rate. Transparency showed moderate representation and was mainly associated with explainability-related discussion. Patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact showed the weakest representation, while safety, innovation and progress, and collaboration and partnership received comparatively less attention. Friedman and Holm-adjusted pairwise analyses confirmed significant differences among themes. These findings characterize patterns of ethical-theme representation within the selected healthcare-AI literature corpus. The study proposes measurable indicators to support future healthcare-AI research, governance, and responsible system development.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support academic writing in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. This focused narrative review critically examines selected empirical studies, research syntheses, and institutional guidance published between 2023 and 2026. It distinguishes improvements in AI-assisted texts from evidence of lasting, independent writing competence and considers feedback, critical thinking, learner autonomy, and academic integrity. The discussion incorporates emerging research from Uzbekistan while acknowledging the limited generalizability of individual institutional studies. The synthesis suggests that AI feedback can support revision when students critically evaluate suggestions, verify sources, and retain responsibility for their writing. As a conceptual contribution, the article proposes a five-stage instructional framework comprising independent planning, targeted AI assistance, critical evaluation, student-led revision, and reflection. The framework has not been empirically tested. The article concludes by identifying priorities for responsible classroom implementation and future research in Uzbek higher education.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering managerial decision processes, yet evidence remains fragmented regarding when AI-generated advice should be trusted, how managers should evaluate it, and how decision quality should be assessed. This study systematically reviews GenAI-supported managerial decision-making by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening, bibliometric mapping, author-keyword co-occurrence analysis, thematic synthesis, and the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework. A Scopus export containing 3,500 records was screened using temporal, language, document-type, topical, and contextual criteria, yielding 99 studies published between 2024 and 2026. The final corpus comprises 342 unique authors across 94 publication sources. Four themes dominate: decision augmentation and analytics; trust, governance, and explainability; human–AI collaboration and capability; and decision quality and organizational outcomes. Trust is more often represented through governance, transparency, explainability, calibration, and human oversight than as an explicitly measured construct, while AI literacy appears explicitly in only one study. Decision quality is likewise rarely conceptualized directly and is commonly proxied by accuracy, efficiency, or predictive performance. The review proposes an integrative model in which GenAI decision-support capabilities influence managerial decision quality through calibrated trust and human–AI collaboration, with AI literacy functioning as a critical capability for verification and appropriate reliance. The study concludes with a TCCM-based research agenda for human-centered GenAI decision research. Keywords: generative AI; managerial decision-making; trust in AI; AI literacy; decision quality

documents.abstract: The current paper explores how generative artificial intelligence and algorithms change the educational process within the family. The research will explore how the technologies used in contemporary family communications, cognitive development issues, and ethical problems that arise due to the introduction of AI systems into the family learning space. Utilizing the latest theoretical approaches in pedagogical psychology, AI ethics, and family education, the research focuses on the impact of generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and other similar technologies, on home-based learning. Based on the results of the research, the use of artificial intelligence in the learning process can have a significant effect on the ability of children to think independently and develop metacognitive skills.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

documents.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

This presentation examines the hidden costs and long-term implications of vibe coding, an emerging approach to software development in which artificial intelligence generates software implementations from natural-language instructions with limited human review of the resulting source code. While AI-assisted coding can significantly accelerate initial software development and reduce short-term implementation costs, it may introduce substantial challenges related to code quality, technical debt, cybersecurity, software maintainability, and developer competence. The presentation explores the productivity paradox of AI-generated software, highlighting how immediate efficiency gains may be offset by increased maintenance requirements, architectural complexity, code duplication, and difficulties in understanding and modifying generated solutions. Particular attention is devoted to the accumulation of technical debt and its potential to undermine long-term software engineering productivity. Drawing on recent empirical studies and industry reports, the presentation discusses security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, including inadequate access controls, exposure of sensitive information, and the gap between functional correctness and security compliance. It also examines the effects of AI-assisted programming on developers' learning outcomes, the unpredictability of AI service costs, and the risks of vendor lock-in. The presentation concludes by emphasizing the importance of responsible AI-assisted software development, including clear specifications, architectural guidelines, human oversight, systematic code review, rigorous testing, security verification, organizational governance, and continuous professional training.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has reached the administrative core of the universities, where students are recruited, admitted and supported. We call this administrative AI, meaning chatbots, predictive analytics and automated screening applied to administration rather than to teaching. It arrived rapidly, at an uncertain moment for higher education governance. Geopolitical upheaval is troubling student mobility and internationalisation, and universities whose finances depend on international enrolment are discovering how resilient they are. Research has been slow to follow, remaining confined to teaching and learning. Where administrative AI is noticed, it is classified as routine efficiency, far from the politics of mobility or the question of what institutions can govern. We ask three questions here. What motivates higher education institutions (HEIs) to include AI in their administrative services, and what global and geopolitical forces shape those drivers? How do such systems intersect with visa regimes, with regional education hubs, and with the financial exposure of universities that depend on international enrolment? And which governance conditions make administrative AI strengthen institutional resilience, equity and participation, and which let it erode them? Socio-technical systems theory supplies our main lens, with globalisation and diffusion research working behind it. From these perspectives we build a framework of five drivers, which are infrastructural readiness, competitive positioning under enrolment volatility, regulatory and mobility mandates, commercial platform ecosystems and sustainability legitimacy. We give each one a mechanism, a cast of actors and a characteristic risk, and different combinations direct institutions to different paths. Three socio-technical propositions organise the reading, examined against institutional cases and six documented episodes in which administrative or mobility automation failed or faced resistance. We also take up higher education as a site of soft power, automation's effect on staff as well as student mobility, and the leadership capabilities without which governance conditions stay on paper. Our central claim is that administrative AI poses a governance question rather than a merely technical one. Whether it produces resilience or dependency turns on procurement terms, contestability, who takes part, and what gets audited. The technology settles none of it.

Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan otomatisasi telah mengubah secara fundamental tatanan dunia kerja, pola pendidikan, dan model pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. Fenomena disrupsi ini melahirkan tuntutan baru terhadap konsep human capital, dari sekadar modal tenaga kerja fisik menuju konsep “Human Capital 5.0” yang menekankan keselarasan antara kompetensi manusia yang berpusat pada nilai-nilai kemanusiaan (human-centered) dengan kecanggihan teknologi berbasis data (technology-based). Artikel ini bertujuan mengkaji peran pendidikan dan manajemen sumber daya manusia dalam merespons disrupsi AI dan otomatisasi, serta menganalisis kontribusi ekonomi digital dan kecerdasan buatan terhadap kualitas pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Metode yang digunakan adalah studi kepustakaan (library research) dengan pendekatan deskriptif-kualitatif terhadap literatur ilmiah nasional dan internasional. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa pendidikan berperan strategis melalui reorientasi kurikulum berbasis literasi digital, penguatan pembelajaran sepanjang hayat (lifelong learning), dan pengembangan soft skill yang relatif sulit digantikan mesin; sementara manajemen sumber daya manusia berperan melalui strategi reskilling dan upskilling yang selaras dengan kebutuhan industri. Dari sisi ekonomi digital, pemanfaatan AI dan business intelligence terbukti mampu meningkatkan kecepatan, ketepatan, dan akurasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis, khususnya pada sektor Usaha Mikro, Kecil, dan Menengah (UMKM), meskipun kesenjangan akses teknologi dan literasi digital di wilayah kepulauan dan pedesaan seperti Nusa Tenggara Barat masih menjadi tantangan tersendiri. Artikel ini merekomendasikan penguatan sinergi tiga pihak (triple helix) antara lembaga pendidikan, dunia usaha, dan pemerintah daerah untuk membangun ekosistem Human Capital 5.0 yang inklusif, adaptif, dan berkelanjutan. The paper proposes an ethical framework that prioritizes human dignity over excessive data collection and continuous surveillance.

documents.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.

The digital transformation is reshaping the functioning of academic, administrative and human-resource operations in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the implementation of digital HR in the private Universities of India, specifically on the following digital HR practices: payroll automation, employee self-service, online recruitment, digital performance appraisal, learning management systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and HR analytics. The descriptive survey design was adopted and the data were obtained from 60 HR professionals and administrative personnel in private higher education institutions. The results indicate that high adoption of payroll automation and employee self-service portals and on the other hand, AI-based recruitment and HR analytics are still in their early stages. Financial challenges, employee resistance, lack of digital skills, integration of systems and data-security issues are the main challenges identified. The results have shown that the HR automation process in private Universities is moving from simple automation to more sophisticated and data-oriented HR processes; however, sophisticated digital HR is still at its beginning stage. Introduction Recent advances in Artificial intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled more dynamic digital learning experiences. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) leverage this capability to improve learning outcomes by offering structured and responsive support. This paper introduces iLeap Tutor , an intelligent learning platform that delivers consistent, structured, course-aligned learning materials that meet course requirements, such as Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and National E-learning Center (NeLC) standards. Methods iLeap Tutor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the tutor's uploaded course materials together with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (Preview), with prompts that embed the CLO and NeLC requirements, and the tutor reviews and approves the generated course. The platform was evaluated as a single-course proof-of-concept using the Selected Topics in Computer Science course at Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (IAU). The generated content was assessed using BERTScore, Self-BLEU, and latency measurements, and thirteen academic experts evaluated the generated course in terms of content accuracy, alignment with CLOs, structure, language quality, and platform usability. Results The evaluation achieved a BERTScore-F1 of 0.829 and a cross-run Self-BLEU result of 0.553 and a within-lesson Self-BLEU of 0.146, while the generation of 16 course topics averaged 219 s in latency. At least 92.3% of responses on every questionnaire item indicated agreement, and all of them would recommend the platform. Discussion The results indicate strong semantic alignment and output consistency across multiple runs and within-lesson content diversity.

documents.abstract: This study aims to improve the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang through the implementation of gamified learning using the Blooket game. The main problem underlying this research is the low level of students’ reading comprehension, characterized by difficulties in understanding texts, low learning motivation, and limited student engagement due to the use of conventional teaching methods. This research employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) approach based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles. The research subjects were 14 third-grade students of SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Data were collected through reading comprehension tests, observation sheets, motivation questionnaires, and interviews. The data were analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The results of the study indicate that the implementation of gamification through Blooket significantly improves students’ reading comprehension. This improvement is evident from the increase in students’ average reading comprehension scores from the pre-cycle to Cycle I and further improvement in Cycle II. In addition, the use of Blooket enhances students’ intrinsic motivation and engagement in reading activities. Supporting factors include attractive visual displays, point and ranking systems, and instant feedback provided by the Blooket platform. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that gamified learning using the Blooket game is effective in improving the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Therefore, Blooket can be used as an innovative alternative learning media in Indonesian language instruction at the elementary school level.

New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

As technology continues to advance and enterprises increasingly deploy innovative digital technologies to power and transform their business processes, Smart Organizations are adopting Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) to automate, optimize, and enhance operational performance in the digital age. Unlike conventional AI systems that primarily execute predefined tasks and provide analytical insights, Agentic AI possesses autonomous decision-making, adaptive learning, goal-oriented reasoning, and proactive execution capabilities that enable organizations to respond dynamically to changing business environments. Within the context of Industry 5.0, which emphasizes human-centricity, sustainability, resilience, and intelligent collaboration between humans and machines, Agentic AI is emerging as a strategic enabler of business optimization and organizational transformation. This study explores the adoption of Agentic AI within industry 5.0 Smart Organizations and examines its impact on operational efficiency, decision-making quality, workforce productivity, customer experience, supply chain performance, and organizational resilience. Drawing upon Human–AI Collaboration Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and Industry 5.0 principles, the research proposes a conceptual framework that integrates autonomous AI agents, human expertise, and digital enterprise ecosystems to create adaptive and self-optimizing organizations. The study further investigates the critical success factors influencing Agentic AI adoption, including technological readiness, organizational culture, governance structures, workforce competencies, data infrastructure, and ethical considerations. The findings demonstrate that Agentic AI significantly contributes to business optimization by reducing operational inefficiencies, improving resource utilization, accelerating decision cycles, enhancing predictive capabilities, and enabling continuous process improvement. Furthermore, the research argues that the convergence of Industry 5.0 and Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from traditional automation toward autonomous, collaborative, and intelligent enterprise ecosystems where humans and AI agents work synergistically to generate sustainable business value. The study contributes to the emerging body of knowledge on Industry 5.0 by providing theoretical and practical insights into how Smart Organizations can strategically leverage Agentic AI to achieve competitive advantage, organizational agility, and long-term business sustainability in the age of artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: In the context of foreign language writing, studies suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning supports knowledge acquisition and increases motivation (Chen & Gong, 2025). However, its use requires a meticulous implementation due to deficiencies in academic rigor and citation accuracy, as well as the risk of over-reliance (Chen & Gong, 2025; Solak, 2024). Through a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-intervention measures, this study evaluates the efficacy of a GenAI-mediated pedagogical sequence on argumentative writing performance. Following a process-based writing approach (Flower & Hayes, 1981), 39 second-year English Language Teaching (ELT) students participated in five sessions focused on self-assessment and draft editing. These sessions were assisted by tools such as Gemin (for IELTS rubric-based draft evaluation), Quillbot (for grammar and style correction), and Lextutor (for lexical profiling). The results confirm that GenAI —when integrated into a structured sequence— seems to strengthen L2 writing clarity, making it more precise and readable by optimizing feedback and promoting the critical, self-regulated use of these tools for essay improvement. Furthermore, the high level of student satisfaction with the resources used highlights the importance of fostering digital literacy and enhancing the role of GenAI as a pedagogical complement. This approach promotes the ethical integration of emerging technologies into writing instruction within Higher Education.

The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education programming raises questions about its influence on learning autonomy and critical thinking. This stems from theoretical concerns about technological dependency and from the limited regional empirical evidence on how these effects vary by experience level. This quantitative study examines whether experience level (novices vs. advanced) and AI usage frequency associate with these constructs among computer science students in Costa Rica. Using a cross-sectional design, 99 students from Universidad Hispanoamericana de Costa Rica were classified as novices (n = 79) or advanced (n = 20), via the Dreyfus & Dreyfus (1986) model with 5 weighted indicators. Accordingly, autonomy (а = 0,685) and critical thinking (а = 0,742) were measured, and both constructs were analyzed using Welch t-tests, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression. Autonomy showed suggestive evidence of being higher in advanced students [t(49,2) = 2,079, p = 0,043, g = 0,386], though nonparametric analysis did not confirm this [U = 614,5, p = 0,125]. Critical thinking showed no significant difference [t(42,1) = 1,816, p = 0,077, g = 0,361], and AI usage frequency was not associated with autonomy [r = 0,166, p = 0,101] or critical thinking [r = 0,123, p = 0,226]. Both constructs showed robust correlation [r = 0,552, p < 0,001; р = 0,533, p < 0,001]. The 88,9 % active modification rate suggests students use AI as cognitive support, potentially explaining the null associations. Given that 85,9 % support regulated use and 10,1 % favor prohibition, these preliminary findings suggest that promoting ethical regulated AI use may be preferable to restriction.

As generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools become increasingly integrated into language education, understanding how learners respond to AI-generated feedback during writing revision has become an important research concern. Existing studies have primarily examined the effects of AI on writing performance, with less attention to learners’ reported decision-making and reflection during revision. This qualitative study investigated learner-AI interaction, reported revision practices and learner perceptions among 18 first-year non-English-major students enrolled in a university EFL writing course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews following a Gen AI-assisted revision task and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings identified three interaction patterns with Gen AI: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, metacognitive AI engagement. Participants differed in how they evaluated and used AI-generated feedback, including passive acceptance, selective uptake, and critical evaluation. Some reported increased confidence, motivation, and awareness of linguistic form, whereas others expressed concerns about overreliance, authorship, and loss of personal voice. These self-reported experiences provide insight into how EFL learners perceive and manage GenAI-assisted revision, highlighting the need for pedagogical approaches that foster critical AI literacy and reflective learner autonomy.

Current generative AI models solve introductory physics problems at expert level. Kortemeyer (2026) reports that GPT-5 Thinking scores 27/30 on physics finals and 92.3% on a representation translation test, categorizing problems by solution method rather than surface features: a hallmark of expert cognition. As of summer 2026, most standard kinematics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism problems can be solved almost instantaneously. Small accommodations accumulate quietly: allowing AI-generated visualizations here, AI-assisted explanations there. The real danger lies not in incorrect outputs, but in the gradual erosion of students' engagement in epistemic practices: the ways of thinking, predicting, and evaluating evidence that define scientific reasoning. Kortemeyer calls this the "boiling frog problem": educational systems may adapt so incrementally to AI capabilities that their foundational learning goals are no longer questioned until it is too late to reverse course. This paper proposes a constructive, classroom-ready answer at the level of individual instructional design. It presents AIRIS as a deliberately practice-oriented condensation of a broader, more fine-grained theoretical account of how cognitive regulation is distributed in hybrid human-AI cognition. Drawing on research in self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence, AIRIS structures student work across three phases: before, during, and after AI use. The relevant question is not whether AI augments performance (it undeniably does), but whether that augmentation enhances or displaces the cognitive work essential to learning. The answer lies not in the tool, but in the task.

This narrative literature review examines how knowledge acquisition methods may shape conceptual mastery in private institutions of learning in Uganda. It examines and brings together the conceptual and theoretical perspectives represented in the literature cited by different authors, including constructivist learning, deep approaches to learning, critical thinking, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, experiential learning, formative assessment, and technology-supported instruction. The review also looks at the advantages and disadvantages of artificial intelligence and digital knowledge-management tools. The reviewed literature consistently argues that conceptual mastery occurs when learners actively connect new material with prior knowledge, explain ideas, investigate problems, receive feedback, reflect on their learning, and transfer knowledge to authentic tasks. Large language models (LLMs) are emerging enablers of industrial information integration, yet their adoption mechanisms in construction remain unclear. This study develops an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model and the Information Systems Success model, extended with trust, prior LLM experience, perceived substitution crisis, and job specialization, to explain individual adoption of LLMs for information integration in construction. Data from a cross-sectional survey of 82 Chinese construction professionals are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Results show that perceived ease of use robustly strengthens attitude and provides directional evidence for strengthening perceived usefulness, while perceived usefulness strengthens attitude and attitude drives intention to use. Trust, reinforced by perceived information quality, shows a positive association with intention under the primary one-tailed criterion, but this relationship requires further validation under the two-tailed robustness check. System quality and information quality indirectly foster adoption by improving perceived ease of use, although the relationship between system quality and trust is supported only as directional evidence, while prior LLM experience enhances ease of use but not perceived usefulness or trust. Perceived substitution crisis and job specialization exhibit no significant effects. The findings highlight that successful LLM-enabled information integration depends on both technical quality and psychological appraisals, and they offer implications for designing trustworthy, humancentered LLM applications that advance intelligent, interconnected construction ecosystems. The study links micro-level user acceptance with macro-level digital transformation and integration strategic objectives.

This theoretical paper examines how educational leaders can leverage generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for equity-focused school and district improvement. Although prior improvement leadership research connects equity-focused leadership, improvement science, and workplace culture (Shepard, 2026), AI use in education remains largely focused on individual use, leaving less understood about what changes when GenAI becomes part of an improvement team. Drawing on equity-focused leadership, improvement science, workplace culture, and human-AI teaming, the paper introduces the Human-AI Team Improvement Framework. The framework centers equity-focused collaborative continuous improvement and identifies three interdependent leadership conditions (co-inquiry, empowered ownership, and courageous safety) that support humans and GenAI in working, learning, and improving together. The framework focuses attention on the leadership conditions needed for human-AI teams to work and learn together in improvement. It suggests that GenAI may help teams address immediate problems while also building their capacity to inquire, learn, and improve. The paper concludes with implications for educational leaders and directions for research on human-AI improvement teams in practice.

Most school responses to generative AI begin with tools: which platform to license, which training day to run, which policy to publish. This article argues that the order is backwards. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on curriculum reform and institutional change, it examines AI in schools as a leadership problem. It sets out five pressures that leaders face: a speed gap between students' adoption of AI and institutions' capacity to govern it; a purpose question about what school is for when knowledge is freely available; an ecosystem problem, in which reforms fail not at the design stage but in the system of assessment, professional learning and routines they land in; a sequencing problem, in which institutions buy tools before doing the human work that makes them useful; and a structural shift in which families increasingly unbundle schooling. It proposes a five-step leadership sequence (purpose, conversation, red lines, ecosystem align‐ ment and iteration) and argues that leaders should separate two decisions that are usually treated as one: what AI should free time for, and how fast the institution should move.

Debate about generative AI in education often asks whether it is good or bad for learning. A 2026 expert consensus report from the University of Minnesota, UNC-Chapel Hill and UC Irvine argues that this question is too blunt. Thirty experts used a preregistered Delphi method to rate 65 learning processes for how likely general-purpose generative AI is to enhance or disrupt them, reaching consensus on 42. The pattern they describe can be read as a sequence: AI threatens the early work of taking in new information, can support the consolidation of what has been learned, and does not yet reliably support higher-order thinking and transfer. The report also rates the strength of the existing evidence as low. This review asks whether the experimental and observational studies published so far are consistent with that consensus. It maps a field experiment with high-school mathematics students, a randomised con‐ trolled trial of an AI physics tutor, an EEG study of essay writing, and survey research on cognitive offloading onto the three stages of the sequence. The studies largely agree with the experts. Unrestricted answer-giving harms acquisition. Tutor-style designs built on learning science can strengthen consolidation. Offloading thinking is linked with weaker critical thinking. We summarise this as a 'learn first, then use AI' principle, link it to established learning science, and set out implications for teachers, school leaders and researchers.

Abstract Courts are adopting artificial intelligence faster than lawmakers are writing rules for it. Risk scores inform bail and sentencing, language models draft summaries and sometimes reasoning, and judicial councils issue guidance in the absence of statutes. This article asks what a litigant is legally entitled to when an AI system touches the decision that affects them. Using a doctrinal and functional comparative method, we examine binding and soft-law instruments from the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, Brazil, Colombia and India, checked against official or reliable sources as of 26 October 2026. Three findings emerge. First, transparency duties are mostly addressed to institutions and regulators; the person whose liberty or rights are at stake rarely gets a right to know that AI was used, still less how. Second, human oversight is declared everywhere but engineered almost nowhere, despite strong evidence that nominal review produces automation bias rather than control. Third, remedies are the weakest link: with few exceptions, no instrument attaches a legal consequence to undisclosed or uncritical reliance on AI. We propose a Disclosure–Oversight–Remedy (DOR) framework that scales safeguards to the way AI is used, from auxiliary support to evaluative input, and prohibits determinative use. The framework converts principles into enforceable procedural entitlements and offers a template for legislators, judicial councils and courts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction Deep-space missions will progressively limit real-time ground support, rapid evacuation and resupply, creating a need for medical capabilities that can operate with graded autonomy. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but terrestrial performance cannot be equated with spaceflight readiness. Methods We conducted a narrative, hypothesis-generating review of literature relevant to AI-enabled space healthcare. Sources were selected iteratively for their contribution to health monitoring, biofluid analysis, medical imaging, clinical decision support or radiation assessment. The review did not use a systematic screening protocol or formal meta-analytic quality assessment; therefore, findings are synthesised qualitatively and claims are calibrated to evidence maturity. Results Evidence was grouped as spaceflight operational use, space-relevant prototype or analogue demonstration, terrestrial clinical validation, terrestrial experimental demonstration, or conceptual transfer. AI may support personalised monitoring, biofluid interpretation, ultrasound acquisition and analysis, radiation forecasting and clinical decision support. However, most cited applications remain terrestrial demonstrations. Key barriers include limited astronaut data, shifted physiological baselines, restricted computation and power, sensor and storage constraints, model drift, explainability, uncertainty management and failure handling. Conclusion AI is most plausibly deployed as one component of an integrated autonomous medical system that combines wearables and biosensors, onboard records, imaging, radiation monitoring, clinical decision support, crew oversight and delayed telemedical consultation. Near-term priorities are prospective validation in mission-relevant analogues, personalised baselines, resource-aware edge deployment, explicit uncertainty thresholds, human override and pre-defined safe fallback procedures. AI should augment rather than replace telemedicine and professional judgement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has expanded rapidly since the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, yet recent development remains insufficiently mapped. This study examines publication growth, thematic change, citation impact, journal profiles and collaboration structure in AI-related research published in four selected journals between 2020 and 2025: Interactive learning environments (ILE), Computers and education: artificial intelligence (CAEAI), Journal of learning analytics (JLA) and International journal of artificial intelligence in education (IJAIED). Because three venues also publish broader educational technology research, 2719 Scopus records were screened using an explicit AI-relevance criterion; 1397 publications were retained and 1322 excluded. AI-relevant output rose from 54 publications in 2020 to 558 in 2025, a 10.3-fold increase and 59.5% compound annual growth rate. Eight predefined lexical themes matched 60.3% of the corpus and therefore provide lower-bound counts; generative AI and large language models grew from 1 publication in 2020–2021 to 307 in 2024–2025 and recorded the largest count among the eight themes. Keyword clustering placed generative AI in the motor-theme quadrant. Co-authorship analysis identified a fragmented prolific core of 74 authors in the largest connected component, divided into eight sub-groups and linked by authors with high betweenness centrality. The findings characterize AI-related literature in these four journals rather than the AIED field as a whole, and the observed growth is temporally associated with, but not shown to be caused by, the release of ChatGPT.

Background: AI is increasingly examined as a tool for science-specific instruction, feedback, inquiry and teacher preparation, but research designs and claimed outcomes vary. Methods: This systematic literature review applied PRISMA 2020 reporting to a title-only Scopus search through Watase Uake on 5 September 2026. Two phrases retrieved 123 and 114 raw records, respectively (237 total). Searches were restricted to Q1 journal publications dated 2023–2026. The initial selection retained 49 articles; eight were removed in a subsequent science-education relevance audit. Two further Q1-indexed Scopus reports identified outside the Watase export were assessed but excluded as unrelated plant-science research. The final corpus comprised 41 articles, synthesized descriptively and thematically with study designs differentiated. Results: The literature describes AI as a scaffold for inquiry, dialogic science reasoning, multimodal representation, feedback, learning analytics and science-teacher preparation. Some primary studies report context-dependent benefits for measured learning outcomes, but findings cannot be generalized across heterogeneous designs. Conclusions: Appropriate science-specific pedagogy, human–AI interaction, teacher competence and ethical oversight are central considerations.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The importance of the psychometric properties of measures in applied and basic research in the social sciences, particularly in psychology, seems to have increased with the widespread access to these procedures and their growing dissemination worldwide. Nonetheless, the availability and use of these measures may be problematic for researchers. In this paper, we propose the concept of measurement validity induction as a conceptual tool to describe the omission or inappropriate application of measurement validity results obtained in one context to justify the use and interpretation of the same measures in different contexts. In general, this involves the risk of using irrelevant information to justify the use or interpretation of a measure, that is, advocating for validity when it may not exist. Several examples from the published literature on scale validations are analyzed to detect measurement validity induction in the areas of clinical practice, occupational health, and user satisfaction. With this definition (measurement validity induction), we argue for the need to report minimum parameters of the validity of a measure in a new context beyond those reported in manuals or previous studies.
